messages.subject: confusing help information for partitionBy and *ByKey functions
messages.subject_clean: confusing help information for partitionBy and *ByKey functions
messages.body_plain:
The info in the Rd files for both partitionBy and the various *ByKey functions indicate that they take an RDD of list(K,V) elements. This of course makes sense.

However, the example code with each of these help pages has the RDD be an RDD where each element is a simple R vector.

E.g., from partitionBy there are 3 elements, each a vector not a list:

pairs <- list(c(1, 2), c(1.1, 3), c(1, 4))
     rdd <- parallelize(sc, pairs)

I presume that when partitionBy sees a vector and not a list that it just coerces the vector to be a list, but presenting it this way may confuse users.

Given all this, I think it would make sense to have the example  be as follows:
pairs <- list(list(1, 2), list(1.1, 3), list(1, 4))
     rdd <- parallelize(sc, pairs)

Similar comment for {count,group,combine,reduce}ByKey.

-chris

I'm doing some basic manipulation with a 10 Gb dataset split into 22 CSV files and loaded onto HDFS. The dataset has about 123 million observations.

In reading in as a text file, caching, some basic filtering, etc., I'm often getting Java messages about lost tasks and lost executors. This seems to happen in a non-systematic way - I can rerun the same code after restarting R/SparkR and the error may disappear or appear. In some cases I seem to get a valid result despite this and in other cases I don't.

This is using Spark 1.1.0 on a 12-worker cluster on EC2.  I'm starting R/SparkR with:
MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR

messages.subject: Re: confusing help information for partitionBy and *ByKey functions
messages.subject_clean: confusing help information for partitionBy and *ByKey functions
messages.body_plain:
You are right that the help text doesn't match the example. However I think the right solution is to modify the text to say that we support lists of vectors and and lists of lists etc. (I think there might be a nice way to describe these). I filed SPARKR-170 to track this

Thanks
Shivaram

On Wed, Jan 7, 2015 at 3:45 PM, <paci...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

> The info in the Rd files for both partitionBy and the various *ByKey functions indicate that they take an RDD of list(K,V) elements. This of course makes sense.
>
> However, the example code with each of these help pages has the RDD be an RDD where each element is a simple R vector.
>
> E.g., from partitionBy there are 3 elements, each a vector not a list:
>
> pairs <- list(c(1, 2), c(1.1, 3), c(1, 4))
>      rdd <- parallelize(sc, pairs)
>
> I presume that when partitionBy sees a vector and not a list that it just coerces the vector to be a list, but presenting it this way may confuse users.
>
> Given all this, I think it would make sense to have the example  be as follows:
> pairs <- list(list(1, 2), list(1.1, 3), list(1, 4))
>      rdd <- parallelize(sc, pairs)
>
> Similar comment for {count,group,combine,reduce}ByKey.
>
> -chris

Sure happy to try. By "without the cache", I assume you mean not
caching any of the RDDs, not that I need to change some
setting/configuration of Spark.

I'm assuming that each node is making use of 6 Gb RAM because of my
specification of SPARK_MEM when I invoke SparkR, so I'd be surprised
it is running out of memory given the number of worker nodes (12) and
the size of the full dataset (10 Gb). But perhaps I'm not
understanding something about the inner workings.

chris

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I meant not caching the RDDs. The part about memory usage is just a guess I had given that executors are dying.

The other thing is you could run fewer executors per machine and see if it helps. Basically each executor forks off a R process and each R process uses some memory while doing the computation. Thus, using fewer executors might help in some cases.

You can change this by setting `SPARK_WORKER_CORES` in /root/spark/conf/spark-env.sh but this will need to be copied to all the machines and a Spark restart (i.e. /root/spark-ec2/copy-dir /root/spark/conf; /root/spark/sbin/stop-all.sh; /root/spark/sbin/start-all.sh)

Thanks
Shivaram

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Chris,

1. You can go to the Spark web UI to take a look at the worker stderr logs, see if there is any error reported in R worker
2. SPARK_MEM is used to set the driver memory, not the executor memory. As documented in the SparkR readme, to set the executor memory:
sc <- sparkR.init(master="spark://<master>:7077",
                  sparkEnvir=list(spark.executor.memory="1g"))

messages.body_plain:
Ok, I've done some more exploration. Sorry for the dense post, but
hopefully the detail will be helpful.

Here's the setting. I'm using Spark 1.1.0. Original dataset is about
12 Gb as flat text, less when on the HDFS in bz2 format. It's split
into 22 .bz2 files on the HDFS and while not wildly different in size,
there is some variation in size across the files. I'm using a
12-worker EC2 cluster, each worker has 2 cores and 7.6 Gb RAM.  I'm
calling SparkR as:

MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR

I then do sc.textFile to read in and do filterRDD and map/reduceByKey
operations.

When I do cache the original dataset, I see about 1.3 Gb memory per
partition, and most of the nodes use up to 2.7 Gb as they have 2
partitions assigned (a couple nodes only have one of the 22
partitions, so use less memory).

First a couple background questions:

1)  I'd expect 6 Gb available on each worker, so 6 Gb per executor.
However both in SparkR and when I invoke PySpark without setting
SPARK_MEM, I see in the UI that each executor has 3 Gb available. Can
anyone clarify where the other 3 Gb is?

2) In the UI, I see 12 executors and often see 2 active tasks per
executor, which makes sense. But Shivaram suggested using fewer
executors. When I change SPARK_WORKER_CORES, I still see 12 executors,
but only 1 active task per executor, which makes sense to me given
each node has 2 cores, but seems not to be what Shivaram was
suggesting.

Now some results from trying with and without caching and reducing
SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1.

Case A: My original attempt, with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and with
caching. This causes the executor failure mentioned in the previous
thread.  I am able to cache the initial dataset but then subsequent
operations lead to the failure. I note that there are a couple nodes
with 2.7 Gb or so used by the RDD partitions on those nodes. So an out
of memory problem seems plausible given the availability of only 3 Gb
rather than 6 Gb.  That said, shouldn't Spark/SparkR be robust to this
and automatically fall back to disk instead of failing
catastrophically?

As noted, PySpark handles this dataset and analogous operations just
fine with caching.
When I look at memory used by the RDD for PySpark, the maximum on any
given node is 500 Mb.

So this presumably explains why PySpark is fine. But are the
underlying data structures different for PySpark and SparkR? I thought
both had the data in memory in Java on the back end?

Case B: Do with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 but without caching. Things seem
fine, which seems to implicate memory as the issue.

Case C: Use 24 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and caching. This works fine.

Case D: Use 12 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2, but only cache after
repartitioning so that the RDD is balanced across nodes. This works
fine, with 1.1 Gb of memory used per executor for the cached RDD.

Case E: Change SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1 and use caching. Note that a
given node still uses up to 2.7 Gb for the two partitions of the RDD
assigned to it, and I still see 12 executors, each having 3 Gb
available. Now I'm not seeing all the lost executors as in Case A, but
I do see two lost tasks on one of the executors (after one task

Spark requires a fully qualified HDFS file name so hdfs://localhost:54310/user/sukla/wordcount/input/file01 should be the right way to call it

Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> created an issue

SparkR <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR> /  <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-177> SPARKR-177 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-177>
New R to Java bridge on SparkR driver <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-177>
Issue Type:    New Feature
Assignee:   Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram>
Components:   Internals
Created:   21/Jan/15 3:14 PM
Priority:    Major
Reporter:   Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram>

This issue is to track the development of a new bridge from R to Java to be used on the SparkR driver side. This new bridge will replace the rJava dependency in SparkR and has a number of advantages including
Support for using an existing JVM as the backend: This is required for integration with spark-submit where the R process is not launched first, but is forked from an existing JVM which will be the driver Java process.
Ease of Installation: SparkR no longer has any required dependencies and only needs a java binary to exist in the runtime path.
Serialization / Deserialization: As a part of this we will also develop a set of serialization, deserialization routines that work in both R and Java.

More details can be found in https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hscJX3VAp3GW2h24GvUIP1UXfcq8gmxTqml1dcDuL6I/edit#

This is joint work with Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui>

messages.subject_clean: Execution failure when trying to save or collect a file
messages.body_plain:
Hi SparkR developers,

I'm trying to run a R script that reads a csv file, applies a function and saves output as a file.
The script works file for a test file but fails with the following error for a bigger file (1G, ~13,000,000 lines).

Error in save(list = filteredVars, file = rc, envir = closureEnv) :

  attempting to add too many elements to raw vector

Calls: saveAsTextFile ... getJRDD -> getJRDD -> .local -> getDependencies -> save

Execution halted

I get the above error, while testing this in spark on my local machine.
Following SPARKR-23, I did ensure that I set SPARK_MEM and JAVA_OPTS to remove Java heap space issues.

When I ran the same script on an EC2 Spark cluster, the execution was killed at the same point but didn't print out the above error stack. The spark ec2 cluster was also able to run the script on a small test file.

Code snippet from the script :

sc <- sparkR.init(master="local[*]", sparkEnvir=list(spark.executor.memory="1g", spark.driver.host="my-ip"))

summary_stats = SparkR::collect(summary_rdd) # From unpasted code and collect() executed for this RDD

vitals_rdd = SparkR::textFile(sc, "file:///src/input_vitals.csv")

summary_df = as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, summary_stats))
norm_ip = map(vitals_rdd, function(x) { Norm(x,summary_df)})
saveAsTextFile(norm_ip, "/output/normalize")

Norm <- function(x, summary_df){
  Sys.setlocale("LC_ALL", "C")
  parts <- strsplit(x, ",")[[1]]
  record = list("Variable.Name" = parts[5], "Value" = parts[6],  "age_groups_string" = parts[10])
  summary_values = dplyr::filter(summary_df, variable_name == toString(record$Variable.Name) & age_groups_string == toString(record$age_groups_string))
  record$Value_Normalized = (as.numeric(record$Value) - as.numeric(summary_values$medianHR)) / (0.5 * (as.numeric(summary_values$quartile3_75) - as.numeric(summary_values$quartile1_25)))
  return(record)
}

I am new to R and trying to get a POC working for our team by executing some existing R scripts in Spark. Please let me know there's a better way to make this work with SparkR or if it's possible to execute this. Looks like it's a serializing issue and would like to know if this can be resolved.

Thanks,
Sheryl

All three of them have to run a task on a Spark worker. To run tasks we automatically capture variables used in the closure and serialize them. The error indicates that the closure size is too large and can't be serialized.

Just curious -- how big is summary_stat and summary_df ? You can probably run something like `object.size(summary_stat)` to find out. Can you try with a smaller summary_stat / summary_df ?

Also there might be other variables getting captured (can't say unless I can see the whole script), so you could try to see if there are any other large variables present

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sending a detailed log and the script. Some questions / notes below:

1. From the error message what seems to be happening is that the Java process is running out of memory when trying to serialize the Spark task. From the script I see that SPARK_MEM is commented out -- Could you try this with that set ?

2. One thing I see from the script is that there are a bunch of files being read in the main environment. As I said in the previous email the getDependencies function might not be clever enough to not serialize them (for example in_vitals or in_encounter etc.).
A very hacky workaround for now would be to split this script into two -- a pre-processing script that generates summary_stats and saves it to a file and a second SparkR script that reads in the file and just calls NormalizeToAge.

3. I am not sure I fully understand the breakdown of tasks here. Is it the case that you have a lot of data in inpu_vitals.csv and want to process the normalization in parallel ? SparkR works well when you have a split-apply-combine style application [1] and when the input data is big. Its a good idea to think about what parts of your app need to be parallelized and what parts can be run locally.

[1] http://datasaucer.blogspot.com/2014/09/r-meets-spark-logistic-regression-in-r.html

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Replies below:

1. From the error message what seems to be happening is that the Java process is running out of memory when trying to serialize the Spark task. From the script I see that SPARK_MEM is commented out -- Could you try this with that set ?

- I get the same error with it set inside the script. It was commented out because I later set the environment variable outside on the terminal shell and ran `Rscript ..`.

2. One thing I see from the script is that there are a bunch of files being read in the main environment. As I said in the previous email the getDependencies function might not be clever enough to not serialize them (for example in_vitals or in_encounter etc.).
A very hacky workaround for now would be to split this script into two -- a pre-processing script that generates summary_stats and saves it to a file and a second SparkR script that reads in the file and just calls NormalizeToAge.

- Hmm, okay. Yes, the variables (in_vitals,  in_encounter ..) could be the reason behind the serializing issue. Didn't realize session variables were also being included in the serialization apart from the ones being sent to the closure. Thanks for suggesting the workaround. I will try splitting the steps into separate scripts.

3. I am not sure I fully understand the breakdown of tasks here. Is it the case that you have a lot of data in inpu_vitals.csv and want to process the normalization in parallel ? SparkR works well when you have a split-apply-combine style application [1] and when the input data is big. Its a good idea to think about what parts of your app need to be parallelized and what parts can be run locally.

- Yes, you're right. I wanted to parallelize the normalization of values in the large input file. And then next, build a feature matrix for the clustering algo. We'll certainly put in more thought about the implementation and using the split-apply-combine pattern.
Thanks for the link and for going through the script!

Sheryl

SparkR <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR> /  <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-181> SPARKR-181 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-181>
Capture stderr from worker process and include it in the exception <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-181>
Issue Type:    New Feature
Assignee:   Unassigned
Components:   Internals
Created:   23/Jan/15 4:33 PM
Priority:    Critical
Reporter:   Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram>

Right now the error messages from the R process are piped to the Spark executor's stderr [1] . While running on a cluster this stderr is not easily accessible and the exception one gets from a failed task usually just has some stack trace from the RRDD ([2] has an example). We should buffer some of the stderr in the BaseRRDD class and add a try, catch block that will put R's error message in the exception reported.

[1] https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/blob/master/pkg/src/src/main/scala/edu/berkeley/cs/amplab/sparkr/RRDD.scala#L87

[2] https://groups.google.com/d/msg/sparkr-dev/9GtXi7Jdltk/rLXDDRzjhZoJ

messages.body_plain:
Chris

Apologies for the long delay in getting back on this. I was out at a retreat and sick for a bit and didn't get a chance to go through the detailed email. Replies in line

On Fri, Jan 16, 2015 at 12:02 PM, Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Ok, I've done some more exploration. Sorry for the dense post, but
> hopefully the detail will be helpful.
>
> Here's the setting. I'm using Spark 1.1.0. Original dataset is about
> 12 Gb as flat text, less when on the HDFS in bz2 format. It's split
> into 22 .bz2 files on the HDFS and while not wildly different in size,
> there is some variation in size across the files. I'm using a
> 12-worker EC2 cluster, each worker has 2 cores and 7.6 Gb RAM.  I'm
> calling SparkR as:
> MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR
>
> I then do sc.textFile to read in and do filterRDD and map/reduceByKey
> operations.
>
> When I do cache the original dataset, I see about 1.3 Gb memory per
> partition, and most of the nodes use up to 2.7 Gb as they have 2
> partitions assigned (a couple nodes only have one of the 22
> partitions, so use less memory).
>
> First a couple background questions:
>
> 1)  I'd expect 6 Gb available on each worker, so 6 Gb per executor.
> However both in SparkR and when I invoke PySpark without setting
> SPARK_MEM, I see in the UI that each executor has 3 Gb available. Can
> anyone clarify where the other 3 Gb is?
>

6 Gb is the total memory given to the Spark executor. Of that only 60% is used for caching. The rest of the memory is used as scratch space during computation. The UI only shows memory used / available for caching.

> 2) In the UI, I see 12 executors and often see 2 active tasks per
> executor, which makes sense. But Shivaram suggested using fewer
> executors. When I change SPARK_WORKER_CORES, I still see 12 executors,
> but only 1 active task per executor, which makes sense to me given
> each node has 2 cores, but seems not to be what Shivaram was
> suggesting.
>

 So SPARK_WORKER_CORES controls the number of parallel threads used on a executor and thus controls the number of active tasks. If we set it to 1, there will be 1 active task at a time and this was what I was suggesting before.

> Now some results from trying with and without caching and reducing
> SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1.
>
> Case A: My original attempt, with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and with
> caching. This causes the executor failure mentioned in the previous
> thread.  I am able to cache the initial dataset but then subsequent
> operations lead to the failure. I note that there are a couple nodes
> with 2.7 Gb or so used by the RDD partitions on those nodes. So an out
> of memory problem seems plausible given the availability of only 3 Gb
> rather than 6 Gb.  That said, shouldn't Spark/SparkR be robust to this
> and automatically fall back to disk instead of failing
> catastrophically?
>

SparkR doesn't yet have support for spilling to disk in the middle of a computation.  It assumes that an entire partition of input can be loaded into R and processed.

> As noted, PySpark handles this dataset and analogous operations just
> fine with caching.
> When I look at memory used by the RDD for PySpark, the maximum on any
> given node is 500 Mb.
>
> So this presumably explains why PySpark is fine. But are the
> underlying data structures different for PySpark and SparkR? I thought
> both had the data in memory in Java on the back end?
>

The data in the backend is stored in a serialized format (Java just seems it as byte array). The format is different for each language and in SparkR we use the `serialize` command in R to serialize data. It could very well be that R's format is more inefficient than Python here.

> Case B: Do with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 but without caching. Things seem
> fine, which seems to implicate memory as the issue.
>
> Case C: Use 24 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and caching. This works fine.
>
> Case D: Use 12 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2, but only cache after
> repartitioning so that the RDD is balanced across nodes. This works
> fine, with 1.1 Gb of memory used per executor for the cached RDD.
>
> Case E: Change SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1 and use caching. Note that a
> given node still uses up to 2.7 Gb for the two partitions of the RDD
> assigned to it, and I still see 12 executors, each having 3 Gb
> available. Now I'm not seeing all the lost executors as in Case A, but
> I do see two lost tasks on one of the executors (after one task
> succeeded). The error message is as follows. I let it go for an hour,
> but in that time it wasn't able to complete.
>

The cause for the lost tasks are a little tricky to debug given this output. There error output from R right now is piped through to stderr on the executor and that gets lost while printing in the driver. I opened a JIRA to fix this https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-181 (this is a pretty painful bug). Meanwhile you can see the stderr of a lost task by clicking on the Spark Master WebUI (master_hostname:8080) and on the machine name where the task failed.

Thanks
Shivaram

Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> commented on  SPARKR-183 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-183>

Re: Parallelize collect tests are slow <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-183>

So I figured out the problem last night as I was able to reproduce it in the VM. Turns out what is happening is that on Linux TCP is adding a 40ms ACK latency on every RPC. The reason for this is discussed at http://stackoverflow.com/a/2253620 http://www.boundary.com/blog/2012/05/know-a-delay-nagles-algorithm-and-you
This ends up affecting the parallelize, collect tests badly as we make an RPC for each element (using `get`) and we call collect 72*15 times in this test case.

The 40ms delay is a not good though and I am going to see if I can fix it using some of the tricks mentioned (I couldn't figure out how to set socket options from R yet).
In the meanwhile, we can do two things to improve test performance – (a) can we use `toArray()` on the ArrayList in collect instead of calling `get` for each element ?
(b) we can reduce the number of elements from 72 to something like 22 ?

Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> commented on  SPARKR-183 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-183>

Re: Parallelize collect tests are slow <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-183>

Yeah I tried setting it on the Java side. It doesn't completely help as the R process is the one which delays sending out the RPC. (i.e. the difference between writeBin finishing on the R side and the JVM handler being called is 40ms). I tried a bunch of things today and have the following notes
The Nagle algorithm only seems to kick in after some time i.e. after the first couple of RPCs. So opening a new socket connection for every RPC actually seems to fix things. One option to consider is to have a flag sparkr.reuse.connection that is True by default and that can be set to false if users run into this problem.
I tried to write a small C function call in SparkR (similar to string hash code) that sets the TCP_NODELAY flag for a given file descriptor. Doing this also fixes the problem – however there is no portable method to find the file descriptor for a connection. We can look at things like `/proc` or `lsof` in Linux, but it will not be very portable. We could have a platform type check and use `/proc` as I haven't seen this problem in Mac or Windows machines.
The final option is to write a new connection / socket API in C that lets us set custom options etc. However this will be a bigger effort as we'll need to make it work on all three platforms etc.

Given the state of things I am inclined to go with option 1 and only set the flag to open a new connection every time for the unit tests for now.

Hi,

After splitting the script into two, the SparkR script was able to collect/saveAsTextFile the rdd object. This worked fine and completed execution in my local machine Spark. Thanks!

However, running the same on a AWS EC2 cluster (one master, two nodes), the collect/saveAsTextFile() stage is taking a while to execute and tasks are failing for one executor node. The failing error stack trace is similar to SPARK-30 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-30>
All the tasks for that particular worker node fails within 10-15 seconds with the following error :

java.lang.NullPointerException:
        edu.berkeley.cs.amplab.sparkr.BaseRRDD.compute(RRDD.scala:41)
        org.apache.spark.rdd.RDD.computeOrReadCheckpoint(RDD.scala:262)
        org.apache.spark.rdd.RDD.iterator(RDD.scala:229)
        org.apache.spark.scheduler.ResultTask.runTask(ResultTask.scala:62)

        java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1145)
        java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker.run(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:615)
        java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:745)
The other executor seems to be running the tasks but longer till I kill it from the app UI.

I wasn't able to narrow down the issue after seeing the logs. SparkR is installed in all the nodes (master and executors).
Tailing the executor's logs did show an Association error, so not sure if that's causing the above stack trace:

5/01/27 18:02:12 ERROR remote.EndpointWriter: AssociationError [akka.tcp://sparkWorker@ip-<ip>.us-west-1.compute.internal:44663] -> [akka.tcp://sparkExecutor@ip-<ip>.us-west-1.compute.internal:51316]: Error [Association failed with [akka.tcp://sparkExecutor@ip-<ip>.us-west-1.compute.internal:51316]] [

Thanks.

Sheryl

Re: Develop a serializer&deserializer for R objects in JVM <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-145>

I was taking a look at serialize.R I was wondering two things: first why reinvent the wheel when there is a package like Rprotbuf that implements protocol buffers which are implemented also in java. Second is a speed issue. My experience with a different package is that eventually you have to rewrite the serialization in C++. If you are set on that, than writing a prototype in R is a very good exercise and starting point, as long as you are aware of what lies ahead.

messages.body_plain:
Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> commented on  SPARKR-145 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-145>

Re: Develop a serializer&deserializer for R objects in JVM <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-145>

Thanks Antonio Piccolboni <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=piccolbo> for taking a look. The serializers, deserializers are right now only used in the R to Java bridge which is the control path and not the data path. i.e. These are mostly used to send high-level messages like 'createSparkContext' or 'call rdd.cache' etc. Also in this case we want to serialize, deserialize native Java types (those are the arguments to the functions) and it'll be tricky to wrap every native types in a protobuf message.

For the data path, we are still using R's serialization (i.e. just calling `serialize`) and I do remember that we discussed the performance penalties in using that before. We have a different challenge there as it needs to work with arbitrary types in R. I think we will see some of these performance penalties during the SparkSQL integration and my hope is we can then figure out what parts need to be in C vs R etc.

Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> commented on  SPARKR-1 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-1>

Re: Data Frame abstraction layer for RDD <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-1>

Thanks everybody for your comments on this issue. One of the goals of the SparkR project has been to closely mirror the main Spark project so as to avoid reimplementing things. Most recently there has been a new feature merged into Apache Spark that adds support for DataFrames in Scala and Python SPARK-5097 <https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-5097>.

Thus I think the most natural way forward for SparkR is to integrate with the DataFrame backend in Scala. This will gives us a bunch of advantages where the SparkSQL query optimizer can appropriately optimize the column selections / operations and from an R side we only need to think about translating the operators to match the backing DataFrame.

I'm going to break down some sub-tasks for this effort and link it to this issue. The one catch with this is that the Scala DataFrame is only available in Spark 1.3, so we will probably do development on this in a separate branch and merge the branch in after 1.3 is released.

messages.subject: Re: lost tasks and executors problem
messages.subject_clean: lost tasks and executors problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shivaram, thanks.

I did a bit of testing on the serialization question. I know very
little about serialization so this might be naive, but...

In R, with a vector of 10 million doubles using serialize() to output
to a file produces a file of size 190 Mb and takes about 25 seconds on
my Linux machine.
In Python, using pickle.dump on a numpy array of 10 million doubles
produces a file of size 235 Mb and takes about 10 seconds on my Linux
machine.

Perhaps the serialization for Python in Spark is done differently and
produces much smaller file? If not, then the much greater memory used
by SparkR than PySpark in my example in this thread still seems
strange!

chris

On Fri, Jan 23, 2015 at 4:34 PM, Shivaram Venkataraman

<shivaram.v...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Chris
>
> Apologies for the long delay in getting back on this. I was out at a retreat
> and sick for a bit and didn't get a chance to go through the detailed email.
> Replies in line
>
>
> On Fri, Jan 16, 2015 at 12:02 PM, Chris Paciorek
> <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Ok, I've done some more exploration. Sorry for the dense post, but
>> hopefully the detail will be helpful.
>>
>> Here's the setting. I'm using Spark 1.1.0. Original dataset is about
>> 12 Gb as flat text, less when on the HDFS in bz2 format. It's split
>> into 22 .bz2 files on the HDFS and while not wildly different in size,
>> there is some variation in size across the files. I'm using a
>> 12-worker EC2 cluster, each worker has 2 cores and 7.6 Gb RAM.  I'm
>> calling SparkR as:
>> MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR
>>
>> I then do sc.textFile to read in and do filterRDD and map/reduceByKey
>> operations.
>>
>> When I do cache the original dataset, I see about 1.3 Gb memory per
>> partition, and most of the nodes use up to 2.7 Gb as they have 2
>> partitions assigned (a couple nodes only have one of the 22
>> partitions, so use less memory).
>>
>> First a couple background questions:
>>
>> 1)  I'd expect 6 Gb available on each worker, so 6 Gb per executor.
>> However both in SparkR and when I invoke PySpark without setting
>> SPARK_MEM, I see in the UI that each executor has 3 Gb available. Can
>> anyone clarify where the other 3 Gb is?
>>
> 6 Gb is the total memory given to the Spark executor. Of that only 60% is
> used for caching. The rest of the memory is used as scratch space during
> computation. The UI only shows memory used / available for caching.
>>
>> 2) In the UI, I see 12 executors and often see 2 active tasks per
>> executor, which makes sense. But Shivaram suggested using fewer
>> executors. When I change SPARK_WORKER_CORES, I still see 12 executors,
>> but only 1 active task per executor, which makes sense to me given
>> each node has 2 cores, but seems not to be what Shivaram was
>> suggesting.
>>
>  So SPARK_WORKER_CORES controls the number of parallel threads used on a
> executor and thus controls the number of active tasks. If we set it to 1,
> there will be 1 active task at a time and this was what I was suggesting
> before.
>>
>> Now some results from trying with and without caching and reducing
>> SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1.
>>
>> Case A: My original attempt, with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and with
>> caching. This causes the executor failure mentioned in the previous
>> thread.  I am able to cache the initial dataset but then subsequent
>> operations lead to the failure. I note that there are a couple nodes
>> with 2.7 Gb or so used by the RDD partitions on those nodes. So an out
>> of memory problem seems plausible given the availability of only 3 Gb
>> rather than 6 Gb.  That said, shouldn't Spark/SparkR be robust to this
>> and automatically fall back to disk instead of failing
>> catastrophically?
>>
>>
>
> SparkR doesn't yet have support for spilling to disk in the middle of a
> computation.  It assumes that an entire partition of input can be loaded
> into R and processed.
>>
>> As noted, PySpark handles this dataset and analogous operations just
>> fine with caching.
>> When I look at memory used by the RDD for PySpark, the maximum on any
>> given node is 500 Mb.
>>
>> So this presumably explains why PySpark is fine. But are the
>> underlying data structures different for PySpark and SparkR? I thought
>> both had the data in memory in Java on the back end?
>>
> The data in the backend is stored in a serialized format (Java just seems it
> as byte array). The format is different for each language and in SparkR we
> use the `serialize` command in R to serialize data. It could very well be
> that R's format is more inefficient than Python here.
>
>> Case B: Do with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 but without caching. Things seem
>> fine, which seems to implicate memory as the issue.
>>
>> Case C: Use 24 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and caching. This works fine.
>>
>> Case D: Use 12 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2, but only cache after
>> repartitioning so that the RDD is balanced across nodes. This works
>> fine, with 1.1 Gb of memory used per executor for the cached RDD.
>>
>> Case E: Change SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1 and use caching. Note that a
>> given node still uses up to 2.7 Gb for the two partitions of the RDD
>> assigned to it, and I still see 12 executors, each having 3 Gb
>> available. Now I'm not seeing all the lost executors as in Case A, but
>> I do see two lost tasks on one of the executors (after one task
>> succeeded). The error message is as follows. I let it go for an hour,
>> but in that time it wasn't able to complete.
>>
> The cause for the lost tasks are a little tricky to debug given this output.
> There error output from R right now is piped through to stderr on the
> executor and that gets lost while printing in the driver. I opened a JIRA to
> fix this https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-181 (this is a pretty
> painful bug). Meanwhile you can see the stderr of a lost task by clicking on
> the Spark Master WebUI (master_hostname:8080) and on the machine name where
> the task failed.
>
> Thanks
> Shivaram

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris

Those are certainly interesting numbers -- Looks like on the local test R's serialization is more efficient (but a bit slower).
There are some differences in PySpark and SparkR in terms of serialization and how the data is transferred from JVM to R/Python. In Python the data is batched into small batches while in R we serialize the entire partition into a single byte array.

messages.body_plain:
The dataset is 22 .bz2 files contained in this tarball.
http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/share/paciorek/1987-2008.csvs.tgz

Here are some of the basic things I've been doing in my SparkR code.

hdfs_master <- system("cat /root/ephemeral-hdfs/conf/masters", intern = TRUE)
lines <- cache(textFile(sc, paste0("hdfs://", hdfs_master,
":9000/data/airline")))

count(lines)
take(lines, 5)

sfo_lines = filterRDD(lines, function(line) strsplit(line,
",")[[1]][17] == "SFO")
count(sfo_lines)

createKeyValue <- function(line) {
    vals = strsplit(line, ",")[[1]]
    return(list(paste(vals[17], vals[18], sep = '+'), 1))

  }

routeCount <- collect(reduceByKey(map(lines, createKeyValue), "+", 1L))

routeCount2 <- countByKey(map(lines, createKeyValue))

Also, once I start up the EC2 cluster and am logged in, here is how I
set up SparkR:

echo '#!/bin/bash' > /usr/bin/realpath
echo 'readlink -e $1' >> /usr/bin/realpath
chmod guo+x /usr/bin/realpath

cd /root
wget http://cran.cnr.berkeley.edu/src/contrib/rJava_0.9-6.tar.gz
/root/spark-ec2/copy-dir rJava_0.9-6.tar.gz
R CMD javareconf
tar xvzf rJava_0.9-6.tar.gz; R CMD INSTALL rJava
/root/spark-ec2/copy-dir /usr/bin/realpath
/root/spark/sbin/slaves.sh R CMD javareconf
/root/spark/sbin/slaves.sh R CMD INSTALL ~/rJava_0.9-6.tar.gz

cd /root
git clone https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg.git
cd SparkR-pkg
SPARK_VERSION=1.1.0 ./install-dev.sh
/root/spark-ec2/copy-dir /root/SparkR-pkg

# read data into HDFS:
mkdir /mnt/airline
cd /mnt/airline
wget http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/share/paciorek/1987-2008.csvs.tgz
tar -xvzf 1987-2008.csvs.tgz
export PATH=$PATH:/root/ephemeral-hdfs/bin/
hadoop fs -mkdir /data/airline
hadoop fs -copyFromLocal /mnt/airline/*bz2 /data/airline
hadoop fs -ls /data/airline

# start SparkR
cd /root/SparkR-pkg

MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR

-chris

On Thu, Jan 29, 2015 at 11:32 PM, Shivaram Venkataraman

<shivaram.v...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Chris
>
> Those are certainly interesting numbers -- Looks like on the local test R's
> serialization is more efficient (but a bit slower).
> There are some differences in PySpark and SparkR in terms of serialization
> and how the data is transferred from JVM to R/Python. In Python the data is
> batched into small batches while in R we serialize the entire partition into
> a single byte array.
>
> Anyways I might be able to track this down if you have pointers to the code
> you were using and / or the dataset.
>
> Thanks
> Shivaram
>
> On Thu, Jan 29, 2015 at 3:21 PM, Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu>
> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Shivaram, thanks.
>>
>> I did a bit of testing on the serialization question. I know very
>> little about serialization so this might be naive, but...
>>
>> In R, with a vector of 10 million doubles using serialize() to output
>> to a file produces a file of size 190 Mb and takes about 25 seconds on
>> my Linux machine.
>> In Python, using pickle.dump on a numpy array of 10 million doubles
>> produces a file of size 235 Mb and takes about 10 seconds on my Linux
>> machine.
>>
>> Perhaps the serialization for Python in Spark is done differently and
>> produces much smaller file? If not, then the much greater memory used
>> by SparkR than PySpark in my example in this thread still seems
>> strange!
>>
>>
>> chris
>>
>> On Fri, Jan 23, 2015 at 4:34 PM, Shivaram Venkataraman
>> <shivaram.v...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > Chris
>> >
>> > Apologies for the long delay in getting back on this. I was out at a
>> > retreat
>> > and sick for a bit and didn't get a chance to go through the detailed
>> > email.
>> > Replies in line
>> >
>> >
>> > On Fri, Jan 16, 2015 at 12:02 PM, Chris Paciorek
>> > <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>> >>
>> >> Ok, I've done some more exploration. Sorry for the dense post, but
>> >> hopefully the detail will be helpful.
>> >>
>> >> Here's the setting. I'm using Spark 1.1.0. Original dataset is about
>> >> 12 Gb as flat text, less when on the HDFS in bz2 format. It's split
>> >> into 22 .bz2 files on the HDFS and while not wildly different in size,
>> >> there is some variation in size across the files. I'm using a
>> >> 12-worker EC2 cluster, each worker has 2 cores and 7.6 Gb RAM.  I'm
>> >> calling SparkR as:
>> >> MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR
>> >>
>> >> I then do sc.textFile to read in and do filterRDD and map/reduceByKey
>> >> operations.
>> >>
>> >> When I do cache the original dataset, I see about 1.3 Gb memory per
>> >> partition, and most of the nodes use up to 2.7 Gb as they have 2
>> >> partitions assigned (a couple nodes only have one of the 22
>> >> partitions, so use less memory).
>> >>
>> >> First a couple background questions:
>> >>
>> >> 1)  I'd expect 6 Gb available on each worker, so 6 Gb per executor.
>> >> However both in SparkR and when I invoke PySpark without setting
>> >> SPARK_MEM, I see in the UI that each executor has 3 Gb available. Can
>> >> anyone clarify where the other 3 Gb is?
>> >>
>> > 6 Gb is the total memory given to the Spark executor. Of that only 60%
>> > is
>> > used for caching. The rest of the memory is used as scratch space during
>> > computation. The UI only shows memory used / available for caching.
>> >>
>> >> 2) In the UI, I see 12 executors and often see 2 active tasks per
>> >> executor, which makes sense. But Shivaram suggested using fewer
>> >> executors. When I change SPARK_WORKER_CORES, I still see 12 executors,
>> >> but only 1 active task per executor, which makes sense to me given
>> >> each node has 2 cores, but seems not to be what Shivaram was
>> >> suggesting.
>> >>
>> >  So SPARK_WORKER_CORES controls the number of parallel threads used on a
>> > executor and thus controls the number of active tasks. If we set it to
>> > 1,
>> > there will be 1 active task at a time and this was what I was suggesting
>> > before.
>> >>
>> >> Now some results from trying with and without caching and reducing
>> >> SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1.
>> >>
>> >> Case A: My original attempt, with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and with
>> >> caching. This causes the executor failure mentioned in the previous
>> >> thread.  I am able to cache the initial dataset but then subsequent
>> >> operations lead to the failure. I note that there are a couple nodes
>> >> with 2.7 Gb or so used by the RDD partitions on those nodes. So an out
>> >> of memory problem seems plausible given the availability of only 3 Gb
>> >> rather than 6 Gb.  That said, shouldn't Spark/SparkR be robust to this
>> >> and automatically fall back to disk instead of failing
>> >> catastrophically?
>> >>
>> >>
>> >
>> > SparkR doesn't yet have support for spilling to disk in the middle of a
>> > computation.  It assumes that an entire partition of input can be loaded
>> > into R and processed.
>> >>
>> >> As noted, PySpark handles this dataset and analogous operations just
>> >> fine with caching.
>> >> When I look at memory used by the RDD for PySpark, the maximum on any
>> >> given node is 500 Mb.
>> >>
>> >> So this presumably explains why PySpark is fine. But are the
>> >> underlying data structures different for PySpark and SparkR? I thought
>> >> both had the data in memory in Java on the back end?
>> >>
>> > The data in the backend is stored in a serialized format (Java just
>> > seems it
>> > as byte array). The format is different for each language and in SparkR
>> > we
>> > use the `serialize` command in R to serialize data. It could very well
>> > be
>> > that R's format is more inefficient than Python here.
>> >
>> >> Case B: Do with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 but without caching. Things seem
>> >> fine, which seems to implicate memory as the issue.
>> >>
>> >> Case C: Use 24 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and caching. This works
>> >> fine.
>> >>
>> >> Case D: Use 12 workers, SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2, but only cache after
>> >> repartitioning so that the RDD is balanced across nodes. This works
>> >> fine, with 1.1 Gb of memory used per executor for the cached RDD.
>> >>
>> >> Case E: Change SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1 and use caching. Note that a
>> >> given node still uses up to 2.7 Gb for the two partitions of the RDD
>> >> assigned to it, and I still see 12 executors, each having 3 Gb
>> >> available. Now I'm not seeing all the lost executors as in Case A, but
>> >> I do see two lost tasks on one of the executors (after one task
>> >> succeeded). The error message is as follows. I let it go for an hour,
>> >> but in that time it wasn't able to complete.
>> >>
>> > The cause for the lost tasks are a little tricky to debug given this
>> > output.
>> > There error output from R right now is piped through to stderr on the
>> > executor and that gets lost while printing in the driver. I opened a
>> > JIRA to
>> > fix this https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-181 (this is a
>> > pretty
>> > painful bug). Meanwhile you can see the stderr of a lost task by
>> > clicking on
>> > the Spark Master WebUI (master_hostname:8080) and on the machine name
>> > where
>> > the task failed.
>> >
>> > Thanks
>> > Shivaram

messages.body_plain:
In trying to recreate some earlier results, I'm now getting a problem
with lost executors simply when loading in an RDD from HDFS and
counting the lines in the RDD.

Here's the setting (same as in my other posts). I'm using Spark 1.1.0.
Original dataset is about
12 Gb as flat text, less when on the HDFS in bz2 format. It's split
into 22 .bz2 files on the HDFS and while not wildly different in size,
there is some variation in size across the files. I'm using a
12-worker EC2 cluster, each worker has 2 cores and 7.6 Gb RAM.  I'm
calling SparkR as:
MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR

I then do sc.textFile to read in without caching and then try to use count().

Also note that after having run the code below, I can connect to the
UI at :8080 and see the workers but I cannot connect to the UI at
:4040.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
I just realized that one problem could be the Spark version used in the AMI changed from 1.1 to 1.2 (if you are using the latest scripts from Spark's master branch).

In that case you can do two things: (a) build SparkR for Spark 1.2 or (b) Use the launch scripts from Spark's 1.1 branch which should launch a cluster with Spark 1.1

Thanks
Shivaram

messages.body_snippet:
I tried launching the Spark EC2 cluster using Spark 1.2.0 and then
installing SparkR as
SPARK_VERSION=1.2.0 ./install-dev.sh

I now get the following error as soon as I try to do an operation
(count)

messages.subject: Re: new problem with lost executors
messages.subject_clean: new problem with lost executors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris

This took a while for me to debug, but I think I've found the problem. The basic issue is the Spark Core changed its default hadoop client dependency in 1.2.0 and our build needs to change a bit to handle that.
I've opened https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/146 to fix this

Thanks
Shivaram
